chapter: Last years of the band and reflections
title: What set the band apart: smooth music, standard tunes and staying near the melody
summary: Pillars sums up his philosophy of smooth, popular standards that stay near the melody, avoiding bebop and mixing material so audiences go away happy.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Okay, to sum it up, to bring it to a close, what, aside from the big tone, the large tone quality --
-- of your organization, and what some people described as a pulsating rhythm, is there anything else that you think would characterize your band and set it aside from other bands at the time?

Well, I'll tell you, what actually set our band aside from other bands, that we had what we called a smooth band, see. The band could play smooth music, see. And we -- although the guys in the band would get angry at me, but we stuck to it. We stuck to it. We played -- we never did go too far out, in playing bebop and music like that. We always --

Stayed around the melody. We'd always tell a guy, if you're going to play a solo, play a solo, but by all means let a person know what you're playing, see. At least, if you're going to play three choruses, let one of those choruses identify the song. That doesn't necessarily mean that you're supposed to stay there and play a straight melody, but you can bounce around, you can weave around the melody, see.
And a person -- oh, that's so-and-so, that's my song, oh, yeah. He's playing so-and-so and so-and-so, you see.
Does that sum up your musical philosophy?
Does that sum up your musical philosophy?
Yeah, I think it was really a choice of tunes we played. We always stayed with something popular, something standard. Something popular, something standard, nothing too way out.

You see, there are times when you could play way out, you could play way out. And when you got through playing, people would stand there, looking at you. They wanted to know, what's going on? What's happening? Well, now, you perhaps are pleasing yourself, but, you see, you have a commodity to sell, and what you do, you try to sell that commodity. But in selling that commodity, you try to inject things in that commodity that will inspire the men in your band, too. You don't just lay dead there and lay on one type of song or one type of rhythm all night long. You just mix it up. And when you mix things up, people go away happy. Usually, you'll please the larger percentage of the crowd when you do that.
